strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: using reward-free, mixed-quality, multi-embodiment offline data to improve online visual RL sample efficiency.
The method is simple and plausible: pre-train a multi-embodiment RSSM world model, retrieve task-relevant trajectories for rehearsal, and use a behavior-cloned prior for early exploration guidance.
Empirical scope is unusually broad for visual RL, with 72 tasks across DMControl and Meta-World, plus comparisons to both train-from-scratch baselines and several offline-data baselines.
The ablations support the main design choices: naive pre-training alone is often insufficient, while experience rehearsal and execution guidance each improve difficult exploration tasks.
The paper is generally clear and includes useful implementation details, hyperparameters, compute estimates, and appendix results.
weaknesses: The claimed realism of the non-curated setting is somewhat overstated. For Meta-World, the offline dataset is generated from pretrained task-specific RL agents over the same 50 benchmark tasks used for evaluation, with injected noise. This is reward-free but still highly in-domain and potentially contains target-task behavior, so the setting is closer to unlabeled noisy task data than broad non-curated data.

Novelty is moderate. The core ingredients resemble known ideas: Dreamer/RSSM world-model pretraining, nearest-neighbor retrieval/replay, behavior cloning priors, and JSRL-style guidance. The contribution is mainly in combining them and validating the recipe.

Fairness of baseline comparisons is not fully convincing. Many offline-data baselines are evaluated only on a small representative subset, are modified substantially, or receive prefiltered task-relevant data because they cannot handle the full multi-embodiment dataset. This makes it hard to isolate whether GSA wins due to the world model, retrieval, guidance, or evaluation protocol.
The large 72-task result compares primarily against DrQ-v2 and DreamerV3 from scratch, while the stronger claim of outperforming methods that leverage offline data is supported on far fewer tasks.

The evaluation does not clearly separate sample efficiency from total compute efficiency. GSA uses a 280M-parameter world model and substantial pretraining, but the headline comparisons emphasize only online environment steps.

There is limited evidence for generalization beyond task/embodiment distributions represented in the offline data. The paper acknowledges this, but the title and framing suggest broader generalist capability than demonstrated.

The theoretical analysis is weak and mostly restates assumptions. For example, retrieval is shown to reduce distance under assumptions that essentially define retrieved states as closer, and the execution-guidance proof depends on strong assumptions that the guide policy has uniformly positive advantage.

Only three seeds are used, and several per-task results show regressions or mixed performance relative to baselines; the aggregate score can hide these cases. More statistical analysis would strengthen the claims.
Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript alone: hyperparameters are provided, but code/data release details and exact baseline tuning parity are unclear.
